items.stem: Which of the following best describes "escalation"?
options: Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, as defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention
The moment at which parties perceive a mutually hurting stalemate and a “way out”, so negotiations are more likely to succeed (Zartman)
A process in which a third party helps parties to a conflict negotiate a settlement, without imposing a decision
An increase in the intensity, scope or number of parties of a conflict, such as the move from protest to armed violence
items.answer: An increase in the intensity, scope or number of parties of a conflict, such as the move from protest to armed violence
items.markingKey: D. "escalation" is an increase in the intensity, scope or number of parties of a conflict, such as the move from protest to armed violence.

items.stem: Explain why a mutually hurting stalemate can make negotiations more likely.
items.answer: When neither side expects to win and costs keep rising, leaders may calculate that a negotiated settlement offers more than continued fighting, especially if a mediator offers a “way out”, as in the Mozambique peace of 1992.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When neither side expects to win and costs keep rising, leaders may calculate that a negotiated settlement offers more than continued fighting, especially if a mediator offers a “way out”, as in the Mozambique peace of 1992. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between de-escalation and escalation.
items.answer: Escalation increases the intensity, scope or number of parties in a conflict; de-escalation reduces them through ceasefires, confidence-building measures or negotiation.
items.markingKey: Escalation increases the intensity, scope or number of parties in a conflict; de-escalation reduces them through ceasefires, confidence-building measures or negotiation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the escalation of the Syrian conflict (2011–2015) as an example, explain conflict escalation.
items.answer: Peaceful protests were met with force, armed groups formed, jihadist groups grew and Iran, Russia, Turkey and the USA intervened. Repression, militarisation and foreign involvement increased the number of actors and the intensity of violence, transforming protest into a regional war.
items.markingKey: Context (Peaceful protests were met with force, armed groups formed, jihadist groups grew and Iran, Russia, Turkey and the USA intervened.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Repression, militarisation and foreign involvement increased the number of actors and the intensity of violence, transforming protest into a regional war. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to conflict escalation.

items.stem:
Source C
Parties resolve their conflict only when they are ready to do so – when alternative, usually unilateral, means of achieving a satisfactory result are blocked and the parties feel that they are in an uncomfortable and costly predicament. At that ripe moment, they grab on to proposals that usually have been in the air for a long time.
— I. William Zartman, “The Timing of Peace Initiatives: Hurting Stalemates and Ripe Moments”, Global Review of Ethnopolitics (2001) (extract)

With reference to Source C, explain why the source suggests that the timing of mediation is important. [4]
items.answer: According to the source, parties accept proposals only when unilateral options are blocked and costs are high; mediation before that moment is likely to fail, so mediators need to recognise or help create ripeness.
items.markingKey: According to the source, parties accept proposals only when unilateral options are blocked and costs are high; mediation before that moment is likely to fail, so mediators need to recognise or help create ripeness. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: "A ceasefire means a conflict has been resolved." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A ceasefire halts fighting but does not settle the underlying issues; many ceasefires break down, and resolution requires a political agreement and peacebuilding.
items.markingKey: A ceasefire halts fighting but does not settle the underlying issues; many ceasefires break down, and resolution requires a political agreement and peacebuilding. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Conflicts end only when they become “ripe” for resolution."
items.answer: Ripeness helps explain timing, but conflicts also end through victory, and third parties can help create ripe moments.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Mozambique 1992 and Colombia 2016 followed hurting stalemates; premature mediation in Syria (Annan plan 2012) failed; parties’ perceptions shape willingness to settle. Arguments against: many wars end in military victory (Sri Lanka 2009); mediators can create ripeness through incentives and pressure (Dayton 1995); ripeness is often identified only with hindsight. Supported judgement: Ripeness helps explain timing, but conflicts also end through victory, and third parties can help create ripe moments.

items.stem: Briefly explain why conflicts can escalate even when leaders want to avoid war.
items.answer: Misperception, domestic pressure, commitment to public positions, the actions of hardliners and spoilers, and security dilemmas can push leaders into escalation, as in the spiral of tit-for-tat attacks between Israel and Hezbollah in 2023–24.

items.stem: Explain why de-escalation often requires changes inside the parties as well as between them.
items.answer: Leaders need domestic support to compromise; changes of leadership, shifting public opinion or the marginalisation of hardliners (e.g. Northern Ireland in the 1990s) create space for concessions.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a hurting stalemate and a frozen conflict.
items.answer: A hurting stalemate is a costly deadlock during fighting that can push parties to negotiate; a frozen conflict is one where active fighting has stopped without a settlement, leaving a dispute unresolved for years.
items.markingKey: A hurting stalemate is a costly deadlock during fighting that can push parties to negotiate; a frozen conflict is one where active fighting has stopped without a settlement, leaving a dispute unresolved for years. items.stem: Outline one way in which the Rwandan genocide and UNAMIR (1994) shows the consequences of third-party failure to intervene.

— President Volodymyr Zelensky, address to the UN General Assembly, September 2023 (paraphrased)

With reference to Source D, explain why the position in the source might make a negotiated settlement difficult. [4]
items.answer: Demands for full territorial restoration and accountability conflict with Russia’s occupation and aims; with both sides holding maximal positions there is little bargaining space, so the conflict is not ripe for compromise.
items.markingKey: Demands for full territorial restoration and accountability conflict with Russia’s occupation and aims; with both sides holding maximal positions there is little bargaining space, so the conflict is not ripe for compromise. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem:
Source B
Parties resolve their conflict only when they are ready to do so – when alternative, usually unilateral, means of achieving a satisfactory result are blocked and the parties feel that they are in an uncomfortable and costly predicament. At that ripe moment, they grab on to proposals that usually have been in the air for a long time.
— I. William Zartman, “The Timing of Peace Initiatives: Hurting Stalemates and Ripe Moments”, Global Review of Ethnopolitics (2001) (extract)

Identify three conditions or features of a “ripe moment” described in Source B. [3]
items.answer: parties are ready to resolve the conflict; unilateral means of achieving a result are blocked; the parties are in an uncomfortable and costly predicament and seize proposals already “in the air”
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: parties are ready to resolve the conflict; unilateral means of achieving a result are blocked; the parties are in an uncomfortable and costly predicament and seize proposals already “in the air”. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

Source C
The Libya intervention went far beyond the protection of civilians and became an operation for regime change. This was a lesson: resolutions on protecting civilians can be used as cover for military interference in internal affairs.
— Statement by the Russian representative at the UN Security Council, 2011 (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source C about third-party involvement in conflict. [3]
items.answer: the Libya intervention went beyond the protection of civilians; it became an operation for regime change; protection resolutions can be used as cover for interference
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: the Libya intervention went beyond the protection of civilians; it became an operation for regime change; protection resolutions can be used as cover for interference. items.stem: Using the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024) as an example, explain the influence of external support on conflict outcomes.
items.answer: A rapid offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham captured Aleppo and then Damascus; Bashar al-Assad fled to Moscow after 24 years in power. With Russia focused on Ukraine and Hezbollah weakened, the regime lost the external backing that had sustained it, showing how dependent conflict outcomes were on outside actors.
items.markingKey: Context (A rapid offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham captured Aleppo and then Damascus; Bashar al-Assad fled to Moscow after 24 years in power.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: With Russia focused on Ukraine and Hezbollah weakened, the regime lost the external backing that had sustained it, showing how dependent conflict outcomes were on outside actors. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the influence of external support on conflict outcomes.

items.stem:
Source A
The war in Ukraine has settled into a war of attrition. Neither side can achieve a decisive breakthrough, yet both leaderships believe that time is on their side, and neither is ready to accept the compromises a settlement would require.
— International Crisis Group, commentary on the war in Ukraine (2024) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source A, explain why the situation described in the source may not yet be “ripe” for resolution. [4]
items.answer: There is a stalemate, but the parties do not perceive it as mutually hurting enough or believe they can improve their position over time; without that perception and a “way out”, the conditions for Zartman’s ripeness are not met.
items.markingKey: There is a stalemate, but the parties do not perceive it as mutually hurting enough or believe they can improve their position over time; without that perception and a “way out”, the conditions for Zartman’s ripeness are not met. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Military intervention by third parties does more harm than good."
items.answer: Intervention can prevent atrocities, but it rarely succeeds without clear limited aims, legitimacy and post-conflict commitment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Libya 2011 led to state collapse; Iraq 2003 and Afghanistan show unintended consequences; intervention can prolong wars (Syria). Arguments against: Kosovo 1999 ended ethnic cleansing; Sierra Leone 2000 (British intervention) helped end the war; non-intervention in Rwanda allowed genocide. Supported judgement: Intervention can prevent atrocities, but it rarely succeeds without clear limited aims, legitimacy and post-conflict commitment.

items.stem: "Great-power rivalry is the main obstacle to resolving contemporary conflicts." Discuss.
items.answer: Great-power rivalry blocks multilateral responses, but local dynamics and regional actors are often decisive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Security Council vetoes over Syria and Ukraine; proxy involvement in Yemen and Sudan; competing arms supplies. Arguments against: local grievances and identity drive conflicts (Myanmar); parties themselves reject compromise (Ukraine, Gaza); regional powers (UAE, Iran, Turkey) matter as much. Supported judgement: Great-power rivalry blocks multilateral responses, but local dynamics and regional actors are often decisive. items.stem:
Source B
If humanitarian intervention is, indeed, an unacceptable assault on sovereignty, how should we respond to a Rwanda, to a Srebrenica – to gross and systematic violations of human rights that offend every precept of our common humanity?
— Kofi Annan, UN Secretary-General, We the Peoples: Millennium Report (2000) (extract)

Using evidence from Source B, explain how the source reflects the tension between sovereignty and human rights. [4]
items.answer: Annan contrasts the principle of non-intervention with mass atrocities, suggesting that strict sovereignty cannot justify inaction; this anticipated R2P, which redefined sovereignty as responsibility.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A model of conflict moving through stages – latent conflict, escalation, crisis/violence, stalemate, de-escalation, settlement and post-conflict peacebuilding – which may recur"?
items.answer: conflict cycle
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of conflict cycle.

items.stem: Which UN Security Council resolution of March 2011 authorised “all necessary measures” to protect civilians in Libya?
items.answer: Resolution 1973
items.markingKey: C. Russia and China abstained; NATO airstrikes followed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "proxy war"?
options: Restrictive measures such as asset freezes and travel bans aimed at specific individuals, entities or sectors rather than a whole population
A conflict in which external powers support local parties instead of fighting each other directly, as in Yemen
The moment at which parties perceive a mutually hurting stalemate and a “way out”, so negotiations are more likely to succeed (Zartman)
A conflict that lasts many years with recurring violence and unresolved issues, such as those in Myanmar or Somalia
items.answer: A conflict in which external powers support local parties instead of fighting each other directly, as in Yemen
items.markingKey: B. "proxy war" is a conflict in which external powers support local parties instead of fighting each other directly, as in Yemen.

items.stem: "All conflicts move through the stages of the conflict cycle in the same order." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Real conflicts are non-linear: they may skip stages, return to violence after a settlement (as in South Sudan in 2013) or remain frozen for decades.
items.markingKey: Real conflicts are non-linear: they may skip stages, return to violence after a settlement (as in South Sudan in 2013) or remain frozen for decades. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Military intervention always requires authorisation by the UN Security Council to be lawful." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Under the UN Charter force is lawful with Security Council authorisation or in self-defence (Article 51); NATO’s 1999 Kosovo intervention lacked authorisation and was described by an independent commission as “illegal but legitimate”.
items.markingKey: Under the UN Charter force is lawful with Security Council authorisation or in self-defence (Article 51); NATO’s 1999 Kosovo intervention lacked authorisation and was described by an independent commission as “illegal but legitimate”. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The Syrian civil war was simply a conflict between Assad and ISIS." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It involved the regime, a range of rebel groups, Kurdish forces (SDF), ISIS and other jihadists, and foreign powers including Russia, Iran, Turkey and the USA; Assad’s regime fell in December 2024.
items.markingKey: It involved the regime, a range of rebel groups, Kurdish forces (SDF), ISIS and other jihadists, and foreign powers including Russia, Iran, Turkey and the USA; Assad’s regime fell in December 2024. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a hurting stalemate and a frozen conflict.
items.answer: A hurting stalemate is a costly deadlock during fighting that can push parties to negotiate; a frozen conflict is one where active fighting has stopped without a settlement, leaving a dispute unresolved for years.
items.markingKey: A hurting stalemate is a costly deadlock during fighting that can push parties to negotiate; a frozen conflict is one where active fighting has stopped without a settlement, leaving a dispute unresolved for years. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Mediators must always be neutral." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Some effective mediators are “biased” but have leverage over a party, such as the USA at Camp David (1978) and Dayton (1995).
items.markingKey: Some effective mediators are “biased” but have leverage over a party, such as the USA at Camp David (1978) and Dayton (1995). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the Yemeni conflict has been described as a proxy war.
items.answer: Saudi Arabia and the UAE led a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, while Iran supported the Houthis with weapons and expertise; regional rivalry shaped and prolonged a war rooted in local grievances.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Saudi Arabia and the UAE led a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, while Iran supported the Houthis with weapons and expertise; regional rivalry shaped and prolonged a war rooted in local grievances. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the escalation of the Syrian conflict (2011–2015) and explain what it reveals about conflict escalation.
items.answer: Peaceful protests were met with force, armed groups formed, jihadist groups grew and Iran, Russia, Turkey and the USA intervened. Repression, militarisation and foreign involvement increased the number of actors and the intensity of violence, transforming protest into a regional war.
items.markingKey: Context (Peaceful protests were met with force, armed groups formed, jihadist groups grew and Iran, Russia, Turkey and the USA intervened.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Repression, militarisation and foreign involvement increased the number of actors and the intensity of violence, transforming protest into a regional war. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to conflict escalation.

items.stem: Using the Kosovo intervention (1999) as an example, explain humanitarian intervention and the tension between sovereignty and human rights.
items.answer: NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days without Security Council authorisation, after Serbian forces carried out ethnic cleansing of Kosovo Albanians. The intervention protected Kosovo Albanians but bypassed the UN, raising questions of legality and precedent.
items.markingKey: Context (NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days without Security Council authorisation, after Serbian forces carried out ethnic cleansing of Kosovo Albanians.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The intervention protected Kosovo Albanians but bypassed the UN, raising questions of legality and precedent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to humanitarian intervention and the tension between sovereignty and human rights.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Rohingya crisis (2017) and explain what it reveals about mass atrocity and identity-based violence.
items.answer: Military “clearance operations” in Rakhine State drove over 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh; a UN fact-finding mission called for senior generals to be investigated for genocide. The exclusion of the Rohingya from citizenship (1982 law) and dehumanising narratives preceded large-scale direct violence.

items.stem: Using the Colombian peace process (2012–2016) as an example, explain ripeness and de-escalation.
items.answer: After decades of war, a military stalemate and FARC losses, the government and FARC negotiated in Havana and signed a peace agreement in 2016. Military pressure created a hurting stalemate for the FARC, while the Santos government saw benefits in peace, making the conflict ripe for negotiation.
